than in any other country. The American continent was peopled by two great nations of Europe,
the French and the English. The former were not slow in connecting themselves with the
daughters of the natives, but there was an unfortunate affinity between the Indian character
and their own. Instead of giving the tastes and habits of civilized life to the savages,
the French, too, often grew passionately fond of the state of wild freedom they found them in.

The American continent was peopled by two great nations of Europe, the French and the
English.
The former were not slow in connecting themselves with the daughters of the natives, but there
was an unfortunate affinity between the Indian character and their own.
Instead of giving the tastes and habits of civilized life to the savages, the French,
too, often grew passionately fond of the state of wild freedom they found them in.
They became the most dangerous of the inhabitants of the desert, and won the friendship of the
Indian by exaggerating his vices and his virtues.
M. DeSenninville, the governor of Canada, wrote thus to Louis Ziv in 1685,

nearer to us, but there is every reason to suppose we have been mistaken.

who have lived among them are changed into savages, affecting to dress and live like
them.

most insignificant habits of his forefathers, has remained in the midst of the American
solitudes just what he was in the bosom of European cities.

care the union of his race with theirs.
